chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Ismail ibn Bazi', from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Talha ibn Zayd, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I read in the Book of Ali (peace be upon him): Indeed, God did not take a covenant upon the ignorant ones to seek knowledge until He first took a covenant upon the scholars to impart knowledge to the ignorant ones — because knowledge existed before ignorance.

key_terms.الْجُهَّال: The ignorant ones; those lacking religious knowledge
key_terms.الْعُلَمَاء: The scholars; those possessing religious knowledge
key_terms.بَذْل الْعِلْم: Imparting knowledge freely, giving knowledge generously without withholding
key_terms.عَهْد: Covenant, solemn obligation taken by God from His servants

ai.seo_question: What does the Book of Ali say about the obligation of scholars to teach?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) quotes from the Book of Imam Ali (AS) a profound principle about the asymmetry of religious obligation: before God demands that the ignorant seek knowledge, He first demands that scholars share it. This teaching, preserved in the written compilation attributed to Imam Ali, establishes the social responsibility of the learned toward the unlearned. The original audience, early Shia scholars in Kufa and Medina, would have understood this as a divine precedence obligating them personally to teach before they could expect others to learn. The final clause — 'because knowledge existed before ignorance' — grounds the obligation in a theological principle: knowledge is the primordial state, while ignorance is its absence.
